name: Turbidity sensor module (analog)
description: Optical turbidity (water cloudiness) sensor: an infrared emitter and receiver face each other across a gap in a waterproof probe tip, and suspended particles scatter the light. The adapter board turns the receiver signal into a voltage on its A/D pin: with the D/A switch on A it is an analog 0-4.5 V that falls as turbidity rises (about 4.1 V +/- 0.3 V in clear water at 10-50 C, about 2.5 V at 3000 NTU); on D it is a high/low output with a trimmer threshold. 5 V DC, 40 mA max, response under 500 ms. Sold as: DFRobot Gravity: Analog Turbidity Sensor (SEN0189) adapter board V1.0 with the TS-300B-style probe, 3-pin Gravity header (A/D, VCC, GND), and its common clones.
eli5: A little light shines through the water at a light sensor. Muddy water blocks more light, so the voltage on the A/D pin goes down. Your board turns that voltage into a cloudiness number (NTU).

pins.name: A/D
pins.description: Signal (Gravity pin 1, blue wire). Switch on A: analog 0-4.5 V, falling as turbidity rises (about 4.1 V in clear water). Switch on D: digital high/low set by the trimmer. Above 3.3 V in clear water, so use a divider on an ESP32 or Pico.

pins.name: VCC
pins.description: Supply (Gravity pin 2, red wire), 5 V DC.

supplierQuery: turbidity sensor module analog arduino SEN0189
buildNotes: Header order (DFRobot Gravity 3-pin cable): A/D (blue), VCC (red), GND (black). On the adapter's P1 connector the black GND wire is the one nearest the D/A switch side of the board, then red, then blue.
Plug the probe's own 3-wire cable into P2 the right way round. DFRobot FAQ: a reversed probe cable gives a constant reading of about 0.04 V that never changes.
Set the D/A switch to A for analog readings (turbidity in NTU). On D the pin only gives high/low at the trimmer's threshold.

Power VCC from 5 V (USB 5V / VIN / VBUS). The analog output reaches 4.5 V and is about 4.1 V in clear water, which is above an ESP32 or Pico ADC's 3.3 V. Fit a divider (10 kΩ in series, 20 kΩ to GND) and pass divider=1.5 to the driver.
NTU = -1120.4 V² + 5742.3 V - 4352.9 (DFRobot curve, about 25 °C, valid 2.5-4.2 V). It is approximate: put the probe in clear water and call calibrate() to shift your probe onto the curve.
Only the probe tip is waterproof: keep the top of the probe and the adapter board dry, and keep the probe out of direct sunlight, which adds infrared light.
On the ESP32 use an ADC1 pin (GPIO32-39) with 11 dB attenuation. ADC2 stops working while Wi-Fi is on.

sim.quantity: A/D output voltage (falls as turbidity rises)

example.code:
from turbidity import Turbidity
import time

sensor = Turbidity({A_D})
while True:
    v = sensor.voltage()
    print('V=%.2f NTU=%d' % (v, int(round(sensor.ntu(), -1))))
    time.sleep(1)

test.title: Converts the A/D voltage set on the slider to NTU with DFRobot's curve
